Thereof
thâr-ov'
adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew pronominal suffixes, Greek autou)
A compound of there and of, meaning of that or of it. English once had a full set of these adverbs — thereof, therein, thereon, thereto, thereby — which let a writer refer back to a thing without repeating its name. The Authorized Version uses them constantly because Hebrew does the same work with a single attached suffix.

Biblical Definition

Thereof means of it or belonging to it, and it is the commonest of the compound adverbs in the Authorized Version because Hebrew expresses possession by a suffix rather than a separate word. It carries the first threat in Scripture: “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” — the pronoun pointing back to the one forbidden tree without naming it again. It governs the whole sacrificial law, where the parts of an offering are distinguished with great care: “the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar” (Leviticus 7:2). It measures conquest by territory and its dependencies: “Judah took Gaza with the coast thereof” (Judges 1:18). And it appears in one of the great indictments of the whole earth: “The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant” (Isaiah 24:5). The word is a grammatical convenience, but the convenience is exactly what allows Scripture to speak with precision about a thing and its parts, a land and its people, a law and its penalty.

Webster 1828 Definition

A compound adverb meaning of that, of it, or belonging to it. In Scripture it refers back to a thing already named — the tree and eating thereof, the offering and the blood thereof, the earth and the inhabitants thereof.

expand to see more

THEREOF, adv. [there and of.] Of that; of this; of it.

2. It refers to a thing or subject before mentioned, and saves the repetition of the noun.

3. It belongs to the class of compound adverbs formed with there: therein, thereon, thereto, thereby, therewith.

4. In modern usage it is retained chiefly in legal and scriptural style.

5. In Scripture, the blood thereof shall he sprinkle, Lev. 7; the inhabitants thereof, Isa. 24.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 7:2 — "In the place where they kill the burnt offering shall they kill the trespass offering: and the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar."

Isaiah 24:5 — "The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant."

Judges 1:18 — "Also Judah took Gaza with the coast thereof, and Askelon with the coast thereof, and Ekron with the coast thereof."

Psalm 46:3 — "Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah's charge that the earth is defiled under its inhabitants is now read as an environmental verdict alone, when the prophet gives the cause explicitly and it is moral: transgressed laws, a changed ordinance, a broken everlasting covenant.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that the creation suffers under human sin, not merely under human carelessness. Isaiah 24:5 gives three causes, all of them covenantal, and Paul says the same when he writes that the creature was made subject to vanity and groaneth together until now. Christians who dismiss the state of the earth as no concern of theirs have not read the prophets; Christians who treat it as a purely technical problem have not read them either. Dominion was given to man, and a fallen steward damages what he governs.

The remedy Scripture proposes is not primarily better management but repentance and, finally, redemption — the manifestation of the sons of God, when the creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption. That hope does not license neglect in the meantime; it establishes the ground for care, since what God intends to redeem is not to be despised. The doctrine of dominion in Genesis 1 is a mandate to cultivate and keep, and the sabbath laws in Leviticus extend rest to the land itself. Both stand a long way from either indifference or the deification of nature.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew attaches a pronominal suffix to the noun (-o, -ah) where English needs thereof; Greek uses the genitive autou or autes; the English compound simply joins there to the preposition.

expand to see more

Hebrew suffix -o — his or its, masculine singular; the ordinary way of saying thereof.

Hebrew suffix -ah — her or its, feminine singular; used of lands and cities, which are feminine in Hebrew.

Greek autou (G846) — of him or of it; the genitive that the compound adverb renders.

Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to dwell; its participle gives the inhabitants thereof in Isaiah 24:5.

Saxon þærof — the Old English compound of there and of, source of the English word.

Usage

"Of the one forbidden tree, referred to without naming: in the day that thou eatest thereof (Genesis 2:17)."

"Of a part distinguished from the whole in sacrifice: the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar (Leviticus 7:2)."

"Of a land and the people who defile it: The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof (Isaiah 24:5)."
